content: The vaginal ring, also known as the combined vaginal ring (CVR) or NuvaRing, is a flexible device that a woman inserts into her vagina. It continuously releases two hormones, a progestin and an estrogen, which are similar to the natural hormones progesterone and estrogen found in a woman’s body. These hormones are absorbed through the vaginal wall directly into the bloodstream. The ring is left in place for three weeks and then removed for the fourth week, during which the woman experiences monthly bleeding. Its primary mechanism of action is to prevent ovulation, or the release of eggs from the ovaries. The effectiveness of the vaginal ring depends on proper use. If used as directed, fewer than 1 pregnancy per 100 women occurs in the first year of use. However, with typical use, about 7 pregnancies per 100 women occur in the first year. Fertility returns immediately after discontinuing the ring, and it does not provide protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The method is safe and suitable for nearly all women, including those who have or have not had children, are married or unmarried, are adolescents or over 40 years old, and those who are breastfeeding after a certain period postpartum. To use the vaginal ring, a woman can choose a comfortable position, such as standing with one leg raised, squatting, or lying down. She should press the sides of the ring together and gently push it into her vagina as far as possible. The exact position of the ring is not critical, as the vaginal muscles naturally keep it in place. The ring should remain in place continuously for three weeks, including during daily activities and sexual intercourse. At the end of the third week, the ring is removed and disposed of in a waste receptacle. If the ring is left in for up to four weeks, no special action is needed, but it should not be left out for more than 48 hours during the three-week period. If the ring slips out, it should be rinsed with clean water and reinserted immediately. Side effects of the vaginal ring are expected to be similar to those of combined oral contraceptives (COCs) and may include changes in bleeding patterns, headaches, dizziness, nausea, breast tenderness, weight changes, mood changes, and acne. Known health benefits of COCs, which likely apply to the vaginal ring, include reduced risks of endometrial and ovarian cancer, symptomatic pelvic inflammatory disease, ovarian cysts, and iron-deficiency anemia. They also help alleviate menstrual cramps, heavy bleeding, ovulation pain, and symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and endometriosis. Rare health risks include blood clots, stroke, and heart attack. The progesterone-releasing vaginal ring (PVR) is another option designed for breastfeeding women. It is a soft, flexible silicone ring that releases natural progesterone to prolong lactational amenorrhea (the absence of monthly bleeding) and help space pregnancies. It does not contain estrogen and is used starting 4–9 weeks postpartum. Each ring is kept in place for 90 days, and up to four rings can be used consecutively. The PVR works by preventing ovulation and extending postpartum amenorrhea. It is safe and effective for women who are breastfeeding at least four times per day and whose monthly bleeding has not returned. The method is effective, with 1–2 pregnancies per 100 women in the first year of use, and fertility returns immediately after discontinuation. The lactational amenorrhea method (LAM) is a temporary family planning method based on the natural effect of breastfeeding on fertility. It requires three conditions: the mother’s monthly bleeding has not returned, the baby is fully or nearly fully breastfed and fed frequently day and night, and the baby is less than six months old. LAM works by suppressing ovulation through frequent breastfeeding. It is highly effective when used correctly, with fewer than 1 pregnancy per 100 women in the first six months postpartum. However, it does not protect against STIs, and women should switch to another contraceptive method as soon as any of the three criteria are no longer met. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), also known as morning-after pills, are used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected sex. They work by delaying or preventing ovulation and are most effective when taken as soon as possible after intercourse, up to five days. ECPs do not work if a woman is already pregnant and do not protect against STIs. Side effects may include nausea, abdominal pain, fatigue, headaches, breast tenderness, dizziness, and slight changes in bleeding patterns. Fertility returns immediately after taking ECPs, so women should begin using another contraceptive method to remain protected. Fertility awareness-based (FAB) methods involve identifying the fertile days of a woman’s menstrual cycle to avoid unprotected sex during that time. These methods include calendar-based approaches, such as the Standard Days Method, and symptoms-based methods, such as monitoring cervical secretions or basal body temperature. FAB methods are effective when used correctly, but their success depends on the user’s ability to accurately identify fertile days and avoid unprotected sex during that time. They do not protect against STIs and may be less effective for women with irregular cycles. Male condoms are thin sheaths made of latex or other materials that fit over an erect penis. They are a barrier method of contraception that also provide protection against STIs.
